# Material Lines and Passive Vectors in the Kraichnan-Kazantsev Ensemble

This study investigates the behavior of material lines and passive vectors within the framework of the Kraichnan-Kazantsev ensemble, an idealized model designed to capture the essential features of turbulent flow in the limit of infinite Reynolds number. This model serves as a valuable theoretical laboratory for exploring fundamental questions about advection and transport in highly turbulent conditions, where analytical tractability is often difficult to achieve.

A defining characteristic of the velocity fields in this model is their peculiar mathematical structure. Specifically, the velocity fields are modeled as white-noise in time, meaning they exhibit no temporal correlation, while remaining rough in space—more precisely, they are only Hölder continuous rather than smooth. This combination of temporal irregularity and spatial roughness is what makes the Kraichnan-Kazantsev ensemble both physically relevant to turbulence and mathematically distinctive from classical smooth-flow scenarios.

One of the central contributions of this work is the argument that the phenomenon known as "spontaneous stochasticity" extends naturally to material lines. Spontaneous stochasticity refers to the remarkable property whereby the evolution of transported quantities remains inherently random even in the deterministic limit, a consequence of the non-uniqueness of trajectories arising from the roughness of the velocity field. By demonstrating that this phenomenon applies to material lines, the authors extend our understanding of how geometric structures are advected and deformed within turbulent flows.

Furthermore, the study establishes an important connection between classical conservation laws and the probabilistic structure of the model. In particular, the conservation of circulations—a well-known invariant in ideal fluid dynamics—is shown to generalize into a "martingale property" of the stochastic process that governs the evolution of material lines. This reformulation elevates a deterministic conservation principle into a probabilistic statement, reflecting the fundamentally stochastic nature of transport in the rough velocity fields of the Kraichnan-Kazantsev ensemble. This martingale characterization provides a powerful and rigorous framework for understanding how conserved quantities behave when the underlying dynamics become inherently random.

# Material Lines and Passive Vectors in the Kraichnan-Kazantsev Ensemble: Spontaneous Stochasticity and Martingale Circulation

## Introduction and Motivation

The transport of material lines and passive vectors by turbulent flows lies at the heart of many fundamental problems in fluid dynamics, from the stretching and folding that underlies magnetic dynamo action to the deformation of vortex lines that governs the evolution of turbulent flows. In the limit of infinite Reynolds number, the velocity field becomes spatially rough—it loses the smoothness that would guarantee unique Lagrangian trajectories. This breakdown of classical determinism gives rise to the phenomenon of *spontaneous stochasticity*, whereby fluid particles released from the same initial point follow a random distribution of paths even in the limit of vanishing molecular noise.

To make these ideas precise and analytically tractable, we employ the Kraichnan-Kazantsev ensemble, an idealized model in which the advecting velocity field is Gaussian, delta-correlated in time (white-noise), and possesses a prescribed spatial roughness characteristic of turbulent inertial-range scaling. This model captures the essential feature of real turbulence—the Hölder-continuous, non-Lipschitz velocity field—while remaining amenable to rigorous mathematical treatment through the tools of stochastic analysis.

## Spontaneous Stochasticity for Material Lines

Our first principal result is that spontaneous stochasticity, originally formulated for individual Lagrangian particles, generalizes naturally to extended material objects such as lines. In a smooth velocity field, a material line—a curve advected by the flow—evolves deterministically, with each of its constituent points following a well-defined trajectory. In the rough velocity fields of the Kraichnan-Kazantsev ensemble, this deterministic picture dissolves.

We argue that in the infinite-Reynolds-number limit, an initial material line does not evolve into a single, well-defined curve but rather into a *probability distribution over configurations* of lines. Just as spontaneous stochasticity for particles reflects the explosive separation of nearby trajectories, the stochasticity of material lines reflects the intrinsic unpredictability of how an extended, connected structure is stretched, folded, and deformed by the turbulent flow. The passive vector field that is tangent to such lines—satisfying the same evolution equation as, for example, a frozen-in magnetic field or a vorticity field—inherits this stochastic character. The end result is a stochastic process describing the ensemble of possible line configurations consistent with a given initial condition.

## Circulation Conservation as a Martingale Property

Our second principal result concerns the fate of circulation conservation in the rough-velocity limit. In ideal, smooth flows, Kelvin's circulation theorem guarantees that the circulation around a material loop is exactly conserved as the loop is advected. This conservation law is a cornerstone of classical fluid dynamics and underlies the notion of vortex lines being frozen into the flow.

In the presence of spontaneous stochasticity, exact conservation along individual realizations can no longer be expected, because the material loops themselves become random objects. We argue, however, that circulation conservation does not simply disappear—instead, it is promoted to a *martingale property* of the stochastic process associated with the evolving lines. A martingale is a stochastic process whose conditional expectation at any future time, given the present, equals its present value. In this framework, the circulation ceases to be a pointwise-conserved quantity and becomes conserved *in expectation*: while it fluctuates along any single stochastic realization, its statistical mean is preserved under the dynamics.

This reformulation provides a precise probabilistic statement of what remains of Kelvin's theorem when classical determinism fails. It clarifies how the deterministic conservation law of ideal fluid mechanics is embedded within, and generalized by, the statistical structure of turbulent transport.

## Significance and Outlook

Together, these results offer a coherent probabilistic picture of turbulent transport at infinite Reynolds number. By recognizing that spontaneous stochasticity extends from points to lines and that circulation conservation survives as a martingale property, we bridge the gap between the deterministic conservation laws of ideal fluid dynamics and the intrinsically random behavior of rough turbulent flows. This perspective offers new insight into the statistical mechanics of vortex-line and magnetic-field-line dynamics, and it suggests that the martingale framework may serve as a powerful and general language for describing conservation laws in the presence of spontaneous stochasticity. The Kraichnan-Kazantsev ensemble, by rendering these phenomena analytically accessible, provides a valuable proving ground for conjectures that may ultimately extend to realistic Navier-Stokes turbulence.

# Turbulence and Dynamo Theory: From Reynolds to Kraichnan and Kazantsev

The study of turbulent flows and the amplification of magnetic fields in conducting fluids draws upon foundational contributions from several key figures whose names have become synonymous with the mathematical and physical frameworks used today.

## Reynolds and the Onset of Turbulence

Osborne Reynolds (1842–1912) laid the empirical and conceptual groundwork for modern fluid dynamics. Through his famous pipe-flow experiments, he demonstrated the transition from laminar to turbulent flow and introduced the dimensionless quantity now known as the **Reynolds number**:

$$
\mathrm{Re} = \frac{U L}{\nu}
$$

where $U$ is a characteristic velocity, $L$ a characteristic length scale, and $\nu$ the kinematic viscosity. This ratio of inertial to viscous forces determines the flow regime: low Reynolds numbers correspond to smooth, laminar motion, while high Reynolds numbers signal the chaotic, multiscale behavior characteristic of turbulence. Reynolds also pioneered the decomposition of flow variables into mean and fluctuating components—the basis of **Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS)** equations still central to engineering and geophysical modeling.

## Kraichnan and the Statistical Theory of Turbulence

Robert Kraichnan (1928–2008), once an assistant to Einstein, transformed turbulence into a rigorous problem of statistical field theory. His **direct-interaction approximation (DIA)** provided one of the first systematic closures for the notoriously difficult nonlinear energy transfer among scales.

Kraichnan is perhaps best known today for the **Kraichnan model** of passive scalar advection, in which a scalar field (such as temperature or concentration) is transported by a velocity field that is Gaussian, white-in-time, and self-similar in space. Despite its idealizations, this model is analytically tractable and revealed the origin of **anomalous scaling** and **intermittency**—deviations from classical Kolmogorov predictions. It also illuminated the phenomenon of **two-dimensional turbulence**, where energy cascades inversely toward large scales while enstrophy cascades toward small scales.

## Kazantsev and the Small-Scale Dynamo

Building on the same class of stochastic velocity fields, Andrei Kazantsev formulated in 1968 the seminal theory of the **turbulent (fluctuation) dynamo**. The **Kazantsev model** describes how a weak seed magnetic field is stretched, twisted, and amplified by a random, short-correlated velocity field in an electrically conducting fluid.

By assuming a Gaussian, delta-correlated velocity statistics—closely paralleling Kraichnan's approach—Kazantsev derived a closed equation for the two-point magnetic correlation function. This equation takes the form of a Schrödinger-like eigenvalue problem, whose solutions reveal the conditions under which magnetic energy grows exponentially. The theory predicts a characteristic $k^{3/2}$ magnetic energy spectrum at small scales, now known as the **Kazantsev spectrum**, and establishes a critical **magnetic Reynolds number** above which dynamo action occurs.

## A Unifying Thread

Together, these three names trace an intellectual lineage: Reynolds identified the fundamental parameter governing turbulence, Kraichnan provided the statistical machinery to analyze random advection, and Kazantsev applied that same machinery to magnetic field generation. The **Kraichnan–Kazantsev framework** remains a cornerstone of modern astrophysical dynamo theory, helping explain the origin of magnetic fields in stars, galaxies, and the intracluster medium.

We investigate the statistical geometry of material lines and passive vector fields advected by a turbulent velocity field modeled by the Kraichnan-Kazantsev ensemble—a Gaussian, white-in-time random flow with prescribed spatial correlations characterized by a roughness exponent ξ. While both material lines (tangent vectors satisfying the frozen-in condition) and passive vectors obey formally similar advection equations, we demonstrate that their long-time statistical properties differ markedly due to the distinct roles played by the stretching and compression terms in the vector transport equation.

By deriving closed evolution equations for the two-point correlation functions of the vector fields, we obtain exact analytical results for the growth rates of vector amplitudes and the alignment statistics between the advected fields and the local strain eigendirections. We analyze the small-scale structure of both fields and identify the conditions under which the passive vector correlation function develops a self-similar regime, connecting our results to the kinematic dynamo problem and the growth of magnetic fields in the Kazantsev framework. The critical roughness exponent separating growing and decaying regimes is determined explicitly. # Spontaneous Stochasticity and Circulation in Turbulent Flows

## Spontaneous Stochasticity

**Core concept:** In turbulent flows at infinite Reynolds number (the ideal, inviscid limit), the trajectories of fluid particles become fundamentally non-unique and random—even when the velocity field and initial conditions are specified deterministically. This phenomenon is called **spontaneous stochasticity**.

**Physical basis:** It arises from the **Richardson two-particle dispersion** picture, where particle pairs separate explosively according to Richardson's t³ law. In rough (Hölder-continuous) velocity fields characteristic of turbulence, the classical uniqueness theorem for ODEs (which requires Lipschitz continuity) breaks down. This connects to the theory of stochastic flows developed by researchers like **Kunita** and mathematically explored in the **Kraichnan model** of passive scalar advection.

**Key insight:** Randomness persists in the limit of zero noise/viscosity, rather than vanishing. This is distinct from ordinary chaos, where deterministic predictability is retained in principle.

## Circulation and Its Conservation

**Classical result:** **Kelvin's circulation theorem** states that in ideal (inviscid, barotropic) flows, the circulation around a material loop is conserved as it moves with the fluid.

**The turbulent problem:** At high Reynolds numbers, real flows exhibit anomalous dissipation, and one might expect Kelvin's theorem to fail. The question becomes: *In what sense is circulation conserved or violated in turbulence?*

## Key Research Findings (Eyink and collaborators)

**Gregory Eyink** and coworkers made central contributions bridging these ideas:

1. **Stochastic Kelvin theorem:** Circulation conservation is reformulated in a probabilistic sense. Rather than being conserved for individual loops, the circulation must be **averaged over the random ensemble of stochastic Lagrangian trajectories** generated by spontaneous stochasticity.

2. **Martingale property:** The stochastically-averaged circulation satisfies a generalized conservation law, connecting the martingale property of circulation to turbulence dynamics.

3. **Anomalous behavior:** The apparent violation of Kelvin's theorem in turbulence is understood as a consequence of spontaneous stochasticity—the non-uniqueness of Lagrangian trajectories means circulation is preserved only in the ensemble-averaged sense, not for deterministic material loops.

## Numerical and Theoretical Support

- **Direct numerical simulations (DNS)** have provided evidence for both Richardson dispersion and the stochastic reformulation of circulation.
- Recent work has examined **circulation statistics** revealing area-based scaling and connections to **vortex tube dynamics** and possibly analogies with quantum turbulence.
- The **Constantin–Iyer** stochastic representation of Navier–Stokes provides a rigorous foundation, expressing velocity via averages over stochastic Lagrangian paths.

## Broader Significance

- Links to the **Onsager conjecture** on energy dissipation in weak Euler solutions.
- Connects to modern rigorous work on **weak solutions** and non-uniqueness in the Euler equations (e.g., convex integration methods by **De Lellis, Székelyhidi, Buckmaster, Vicol**).
- Suggests turbulence is fundamentally stochastic even in the deterministic idealized limit, with implications for predictability.

---

**Note:** If you need specific citations, key references include Eyink (2006, 2010), Eyink & Drivas (2015), Bernard–Gawędzki–Kupiainen (1998), and Constantin–Iyer (2008). Let me know if you'd like me to expand on any particular aspect—the mathematical formalism, the connection to weak Euler solutions, or the numerical evidence.

Our findings offer a rigorous statistical interpretation of vortex-line stretching and circulation transport in non-smooth flows, with implications for turbulence modeling and the analysis of stochastic partial differential equations of fluid type.

# Abstract

We investigate the statistical geometry of material lines advected by a class of synthetic turbulent velocity ensembles characterized by white-noise correlations in time and prescribed Hölder continuity in space. Building on the Kraichnan model framework, we consider incompressible Gaussian velocity fields with two-point spatial correlations scaling as $\langle |u(x) - u(y)|^2 \rangle \sim |x-y|^{2h}$ for Hölder exponent $h \in (0,1)$, and analyze the resulting stochastic flow map governing the deformation of infinitesimal and finite material segments.

We establish that for $h < 1$ the velocity field fails to be spatially Lipschitz, leading to a breakdown of deterministic Lagrangian trajectories and the emergence of spontaneous stochasticity: initially coincident material points separate with finite probability in the vanishing-noise limit. Employing multiplicative stochastic calculus and a Feynman–Kac representation for the tangent-vector dynamics, we derive closed evolution equations for the moments of the line-element stretching rate and demonstrate that the mean logarithmic elongation grows linearly in time, yielding a well-defined stochastic Lyapunov exponent $\lambda(h)$ that we compute explicitly as a function of the Hölder regularity and spatial dimension $d$.

Our principal result is a rigorous characterization of the anomalous scaling of material-line length and curvature. We show that the length of an advected curve exhibits multifractal statistics, with the $q$-th order moment scaling as $\langle L^q(t) \rangle \sim \exp[\zeta(q)\, t]$, and we obtain $\zeta(q)$ from the ground-state eigenvalue of an associated non-self-adjoint transfer operator. In the rough limit $h \to 0$ the curvature distribution develops heavy algebraic tails, reflecting the proliferation of near-singular folds, whereas as $h \to 1$ we recover the smooth Batchelor regime with log-normal stretching statistics.

These findings quantify how spatial roughness controls the transition from deterministic to genuinely stochastic material-line evolution, and provide analytically tractable benchmarks for mixing, magnetic-field amplification, and passive-scalar cascades in non-smooth turbulent flows. We conclude by discussing implications for kinematic dynamo theory and the interpretation of Richardson dispersion in the presence of spontaneous stochasticity.
